items.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002
items.q: I first heard Bill Evans... eventually was able to persuade Bill that he should go in to the studio and make a record... We went in and did a basically trio record

ctx.x: Right. Well I have to congratulate you on the contribution you’ve made to the art form called jazz. It’s really quite amazing the things you’ve been involved in and the careers that you have helped.

Well I must admit that I look back on it with a good deal of satisfaction. I’ve been very fortunate because in this business in particular, a lot of the associations that you form, at least initially, are accidental as hell. If someone tells me that I have been helpful to this or that career that’s exactly the thing that I want to hear because I have always looked on the role of the producer in a very specific way. Now one of the hardest things, and I’ve been at it, I’m getting perilously close to my fiftieth…

with doing this. The only real serious variation is that I have — I used to say in recent years — but for a lot of years, a lot of my attention has been focused on reissues and obviously the procedures are a little different there. For the most part that makes it possible to get into cliches like well I spent the whole day in the studio with Louis Armstrong or Duke Ellington or Fats Waller, and he didn’t give me a hard time. But that joke got busted about a year ago because one of my most recent reissue projects…

items.title: Orrin Keepnews — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: we did one record with him, with Bill

ctx.x: But again, the love of this music, that’s what you built your career on. It has driven your career. You are known as a jazz impresario, a jazz advocate, jazz producer, and jazz whatever. You are indelibly, historically, associated with jazz in America.

What I can’t tell you, because it apparently exists somewhere under my surface, I don’t know why and I don’t know how. I do know that the odds were probably against my ever having this exposure. In sort of a semi-accidental way, it began. There also was, remember we’re talking about in the 30’s when there was a hell of a lot of swing music to be heard on the radio. I was, you know, I was ten or twelve years old when that was happening, so that I did have, maybe a subliminal exposure to it. In that sense my timing…

I was in the Air Force and got out in the beginning of 1946. I literally felt that I had been professionally illiterate for the first three years in the service. Since it was a practically automatic thing, as a Columbia College graduate, and I had graduated courtesy of a handful of credits that they were handing out to people who had military service.
